1.pericope_label: The lighting of the lamps and the workmanship of the candlestick

schools.summary: Gill says it is not certain whether this followed immediately upon the offerings of the princes or came at another time, and reports a Jewish commentator's view that God spoke in the night, because then the lamps were lighted and burning; he discusses who was to light them, reporting from a Jewish writer that the office was not incumbent on a high priest alone but belonged also to the common priests, and supposing that Aaron did it himself only because this was the first time, his sons attending and assisting him, in which he was an eminent type of Christ, the great High Priest, who lights the lamps in all his golden candlesticks, the churches, and from whom they have all their light and all the supplies of it; and he notes the fitness of the moment, that God having taken up his residence in the most holy place and the sacrifices having begun on the altar in the outer court, it was proper that the service of the holy place should also be set on foot, since neither the shewbread nor the incense could well be attended to until the lamps were lighted. Calvin says plainly that this precept, like many others, is not inserted in its proper place, Moses again declaring what the use of the candlestick was and how the lamps should be arranged so that their light might be spread through the sanctuary; and he gives his own reason for the arrangement, that God would have the lamps set opposite the candlestick so that the brightness of the gold might shine over against them and the very stand of the light retain its beauty. He marks besides that it is expressly stated Aaron obeyed God's command, as if in no despicable matter, and that the candlestick was made according to the pattern shown in the mount.

Henry observes that directions for making the golden candlestick had been given long before and that it was made according to the pattern shown to Moses in the mount, but that only now were the lamps first ordered to be lighted, when the other furniture began to be used; and he makes Aaron's act doubly representative, since as the people's representative to God he did the office of a servant in God's house, lighting his Master's candle, and as the representative of God to the people he gave them the intimations of God's will and favour, having lately been directed himself to bless them.

Clarke turns the whole to emblem: the candlestick was an emblem of the Church of Christ, the oil of the graces and gifts of the Spirit of God, and the light of those gifts and graces in action among men, so that God builds his Church and sends forth his Spirit to dwell in it, to sanctify and cleanse it, that it may be shown unto the world as his own workmanship; and the seven lights point out the seven Spirits of God, the Holy Ghost being so termed from the variety and abundance of his gifts and influences, seven being used among the Hebrews to denote anything full, complete and perfect. Wesley describes how the lighting was done, the middle lamp kindled from the fire of the altar and the rest one from another, which he takes to signify that all light and knowledge comes from Christ, who has the seven spirits of God figured by the seven lamps of fire; he argues the position of the lamps from the shewbread table on the north and the candlestick standing close to the boards on the south, so that the lights fell on both sides of the sanctuary; and on the workmanship he says the gold was not hollow but solid, beaten out of one piece and not of several pieces joined or soldered together.

Ellicott corrects the rendering of the verb twice, to when thou settest up the lamps and to he set up, and gives the architecture of the holy place: the golden candlestick was placed against the south wall of the Tabernacle, opposite to the table of shewbread, so that its seven branches were parallel to that wall and ran east and west, and consequently the seven lamps, one resting on each branch, threw their light in front of the candlestick towards the north wall, by which arrangement the furniture of the holy place was more effectually lighted than it would have been had the candlestick been placed facing the entrance with its branches north and south. On the candlestick itself he corrects three further renderings, that the clause describes the material of which it was made rather than the workmanship, that the gold was turned or twisted rather than beaten, and that the two limits named are literally its base and its flower or blossom, that is, the whole of the candlestick from its base to its flowers, the several parts being enumerated in the earlier passage. Keil's block on this span is consumed almost entirely by verse quotation and adds only that the choice of the Levites for service in the sanctuary, in place of the first-born, has already been noticed earlier in the book.

debates: Which way the lamps threw their light and why: Ellicott argues it from the architecture, the candlestick against the south wall with branches east and west throwing light northward, which lit the holy place more effectually than the alternative, Wesley reaches the same position from the placing of the shewbread table, and Calvin gives a wholly different reason, that the brightness of the gold might shine and the stand of the light retain its beauty
Whether the verb means to light or to set up: Ellicott alone corrects the rendering twice, while the others take it of the lighting and Wesley describes how it was done

Who was to light the lamps: Gill reports the Jewish view that the office was not incumbent on the high priest alone but belonged also to the common priests, supposing Aaron did it himself only because it was the first time, while Henry makes the act doubly representative, of the people to God and of God to the people

Where the passage belongs: Calvin says the precept, like many others, is not inserted in its proper place, Henry that the lamps were first ordered to be lighted only now, when the other furniture began to be used, and Gill that the time is not certain, reporting a Jewish view that God spoke at night
outliers: Henry's double representation, Aaron doing the office of a servant in God's house by lighting his Master's candle, and giving the people the intimations of God's will and favour

Clarke's emblem of the candlestick as the Church, the oil as the graces and gifts of the Spirit, and the light as those gifts in action among men, with seven denoting among the Hebrews anything full, complete and perfect
Wesley's detail that the middle lamp was kindled from the fire of the altar and the rest one from another, signifying that all light and knowledge comes from Christ
Wesley's gloss on the workmanship, that the gold was not hollow but solid, beaten out of one piece and not of several joined or soldered together
Ellicott's renderings of turned or twisted gold, and of the two limits as the base and the blossom
Calvin's reason for the arrangement, that the very stand of the light might retain its beauty
Gill's typology, that Christ the great High Priest lights the lamps in all his golden candlesticks, the churches
Gill's report of a Jewish commentator that God spoke in the night, because then the lamps were burning

5.pericope_label: The cleansing of the Levites, the water of purifying and the shaving

schools.summary: Calvin holds that though the Levites were not allowed into the sanctuary and were chiefly employed in servile duties, carrying the tabernacle and the sacred vessels, preparing the sacrifices and taking away the ashes, God would have them consecrated by a solemn rite; but lest they should arrogate more than was right he anticipates their presumption three ways, by putting off their consecration for some time, by desiring that they should not be initiated by Moses but by Aaron, and by appointing a different ceremony, since if they had been initiated at the same time as the priests they might have contended to be on an equality with them, and since they were purified only by water and sacrifice without the addition of anointing, the difference in the external rite reminded them that their degree of honour was not the same. He reads the three acts as sprinkling, washing of clothes lest any impurity be anywhere about them, and shaving with a razor, that putting off their flesh they may begin to be new men; a twofold sacrifice is added, and then Aaron in right of the priesthood offers them just like the holy bread or incense, the end being that they should acknowledge they were no longer their own masters. To take them from among the children of Israel is to subtract them from the number of the people, and on this he turns sharply on the Papal clergy, who under this pretext claim immunity that they may live as they like in exemption from the laws, which is not only an unsound deduction but one full of impious mockery, since the ancient priesthood attained its end in Christ and the succession they allege robs Christ of his right. Gill notes that the section is joined to the former, and that the Levites had been mixed among the tribes before the journey from Sinai but were distinguished thenceforward; the separation designs their appointment to their work as ministers to the priests, and as Aaron did not assume the honour of priesthood to himself but was called of God, so the Levites did not take the honour of their office to themselves. The cleansing, he adds, was Aaron's work, by himself or by his order, in which he was a type of Christ, the refiner and purifier of the sons of Levi.

Henry treats the passage as the solemn ordination of the Levites, separated from the children of Israel when they were numbered so that they might be employed in the service of the tabernacle. All Israel must know that they took not this honour to themselves but were called of God to it; nor was it enough that they were distinguished from their neighbours, but they must be solemnly devoted to God. All that are employed for God must be dedicated to him according as the degree of employment is: Christians must be baptized, ministers must be ordained, and we must first give ourselves unto the Lord and then our services. The cleansing he divides between the men themselves, who must wash their clothes and shave all their flesh as the leper did when he was cleansed, causing a razor to pass over all their flesh to clear themselves from the defilement that would not wash off, which teaches all Christians and ministers particularly to cleanse themselves by repentance and mortification from all filthiness of flesh and spirit, since those must be clean that bear the vessels of the Lord; and Moses, who must sprinkle the water of purifying upon them, signifying the application of the blood of Christ to our souls by faith, to purify us from an evil conscience that we may be fit to serve the living God. It is our duty to cleanse ourselves, and God's promise that he will cleanse us.

Clarke takes the water of purifying as water of sin, or water of the sin-offering, made by the ashes of the red heifer with cedar-wood, hyssop and scarlet; since the heifer herself was sacrificed and her blood sprinkled seven times before the tabernacle she may be considered a proper sacrifice for sin, and the water thus prepared rightly termed the water of the sin-offering. The ashes being kept ready at hand for purifying from all legal pollutions, the preparation may be considered a concentration of the essential properties of the sin-offering, which might be resorted to at all times with comparatively little expense or trouble and no loss of time, a mode of purifying at once convenient and inexpensive; the ordinance was therefore undoubtedly instituted before this time though not described until later, and Hebrews shows that these ashes mingled with water were intended to typify the blood of Christ, without the sprinkling of which no conscience can be purged from dead works to serve the living God. Wesley agrees that the water was mixed with the ashes of a red heifer, which therefore may seem to have been prescribed before though it be mentioned after, such kind of transplacings of passages being frequent in scripture; and the shaving of all their flesh he takes as an external rite signifying the cutting off of their inordinate desire of earthly things and that singular purity of heart and life which is required in the ministers of God.

Ellicott observes that as Moses had already officiated in the consecration of the priests, so now, notwithstanding the fact that Aaron and his sons were already consecrated, he is commanded to officiate at the cleansing of the Levites. On the water he renders literally water of sin, or of sin-offering, and notes that as in the case of the holy water no explanation is given of the particular water to be used: the same word describes the bullock offered as a sin-offering at the consecration of Aaron and his sons, the sacrifice appointed for the expiation of sin in Leviticus, and the Levites' own sin-offering later in this chapter. The sin-water evidently denotes the water appointed to be used in the purification of sin, and the reference is probably to the water kept in the brazen laver in front of the Tabernacle, though it is possible that some direction not here recorded may have been given respecting putting the ashes of the sin-offering into water, in which case the sin-offering, not mentioned until verse 8, must have been sacrificed previously to the sprinkling. He renders the shaving literally as causing the razor to pass over all their flesh, a different word from that used of the more complete removal of hair enjoined at the cleansing of the leper, and notes that the bodies of the priests were washed at their consecration and those of the lepers at their cleansing, but the Levites, who were not brought into such immediate contact with the holy things as the priests, were only required to wash their clothes, which was an ordinary preparation for Divine worship. Keil's block on this span is almost wholly verse quotation and adds only that after this purification the Levites were to bring two young bullocks, one with the corresponding meat-offering for a burnt-sacrifice and the other for a sin-offering, and that Moses was then to cause them to draw near before the tabernacle, that is, to enter the court, and to gather the whole congregation together in the persons of their heads and representatives.

debates: Who officiated at the cleansing: Ellicott says Moses is commanded to officiate, as he had at the consecration of the priests, while Calvin makes it one of the three ways God checked the Levites' presumption that they should not be initiated by Moses but by Aaron, and Gill says the cleansing was Aaron's work, by himself or by his order

What the water of purifying was: Clarke and Wesley identify it with the water made from the ashes of the red heifer and conclude that the ordinance must have been instituted earlier than it is described, while Ellicott says no explanation of the particular water is given and thinks the reference probably to the brazen laver, allowing the ashes only as a possibility that would require the sin-offering to precede the sprinkling

Why the consecration was deferred and made different: Calvin gives three grounds, the delay, the transfer from Moses to Aaron, and the altered ceremony without anointing, all to keep the Levites from claiming equality with the priests

What it is to take the Levites from among the children of Israel: Calvin makes it a subtraction from the number of the people and turns it against the immunity claimed by the Papal clergy, while Gill takes it of appointment and separation to their service under the priests

What the shaving signified: Wesley takes it of the cutting off of inordinate desire of earthly things, Calvin of putting off the flesh to begin to be new men, and Ellicott declines the figure, noting only that the word is weaker than the one used of the leper
outliers: Calvin's polemic that the succession alleged by the Papal clergy robs Christ of his right, since the ancient priesthood attained its end in Christ
Clarke's account of the ashes as a concentration of the essential properties of the sin-offering, convenient and inexpensive and available without loss of time
Wesley's rule that such transplacings of passages are frequent in scripture
Henry's note that the razor cleared the defilement which would not wash off, and that those must be clean that bear the vessels of the Lord
Ellicott's observation that the priests and the lepers were washed bodily but the Levites only had to wash their clothes, the ordinary preparation for worship
Gill's typology of Aaron as the refiner and purifier of the sons of Levi
Calvin's note that the absence of anointing itself reminded the Levites that their degree of honour was not the same

8.pericope_label: The sin-offering, the laying on of hands and the waving of the Levites

schools.summary: Gill reports the rabbinic dispute over the age of the bullock, gathering from the second one named in the next clause that it was two years old, though the wise men say one of three years old is fit for such a sacrifice and others say four or five, the decision going according to the wise men. On the bringing of the Levites he is precise about place: they were brought not outside the tabernacle but within it, in the court or at least at the door where the altar of burnt offering stood, on which sacrifices for them were now to be offered, and then from that door to the altar of burnt offering, where the Lord was in some sense present to accept the sacrifices offered to him. On the offering he prefers the rendering wave: they were not actually waved and moved to and fro by Aaron, which could not be done by him, though it is possible he might make such a motion himself and they might do the like after him, thereby signifying that they belonged to the Lord of the whole earth. Some think this testified their readiness to serve the Lord, to which he adds their constant employment in his service, being always in motion and doing one piece of service or another continually, as the people of God and especially the ministers of the word should be always abounding in the work of the Lord; and he reports that Ainsworth supposes the troubles and afflictions of the ministers of God to be figured by the waving instead.

Wesley explains the choice of victim, that it is the same sacrifice which was offered for a sin-offering for the whole congregation, because the Levites came in the stead of all the first-born, who did in a manner represent the whole congregation. On the laying on of hands he says it was not done by all the children of Israel, which was impossible, but by some in the name of all, the princes or chiefs of each tribe, who used to transact things in the name of their tribes; and by it they signified their transferring that right of ministering to God from the first-born, in whose hands it formerly was, to the Levites, and their entire resignation and dedication of them to God's service. On the wave-offering he agrees with Gill that Aaron did not wave them, which he could not do, but caused them to imitate that motion and to wave themselves toward the several parts of the world, whereby they might signify their readiness to serve God according to their capacity wheresoever they should be. Clarke takes the laying on of hands as the one place in the passage where a modern question arises: it has been argued from this that the congregation had a part in the appointment of their own ministers, and that this was done by the imposition of hands; however that may be, what was done on this occasion meant no more than that the people gave up this whole tribe to God in place of their first-born, and that by this act they bound themselves to provide for them who, because of their sacred service, could follow no secular work. Surely it was right, he adds, that they who served the altar should live by the altar; the ministers of God perform offices for the people which the people cannot perform for themselves, and nothing can be more reasonable than that the people should give them the necessaries and comforts of life while they are thus employed in their behalf.

Keil traces the sequence: Moses was to cause the Levites to draw near before the tabernacle, that is, to enter the court, and to gather the whole congregation of Israel together in the persons of their heads and representatives; after this the Levites were to come before Jehovah, that is, in front of the altar, and the children of Israel, that is, the tribe-princes in the name of the Israelites, were to lay their hands upon them. This he insists was not merely, as Knobel held, a sign that they released them from the possession of the nation and assigned and handed them over to Jehovah, but was meant by this symbolical act to transfer to the Levites the obligation resting upon the whole nation to serve the Lord in the persons of its first-born sons, and to present them to the Lord as representatives of the first-born of Israel, to serve him as living sacrifices. The transfer was to be completed by Aaron's waving the Levites as a wave-offering before Jehovah on behalf of the children of Israel, offering them symbolically to the Lord as a sacrifice presented on the part of the Israelites; the ceremony of waving consisted no doubt in his conducting the Levites solemnly up to the altar and then back again, and its design is given in the verse itself, that they might be to perform the service of Jehovah. Ellicott glosses the whole assembly as, here as elsewhere, the representatives of the people, and notes that the phrase used of the laying on of hands is the same used of the offerer who was required to lay his hand upon the victim which he offered in sacrifice, so that by this symbolical act the obligation which rested upon the whole nation in regard to the dedication of the first-born was transferred to the Levites, who were thenceforth to be dedicated to the service of the Lord and given over to the priests as the representatives of the Lord. He renders the offering literally as Aaron waving the Levites as a wave-offering, observes that the manner in which they were thus set apart is not expressed and may have been done by leading them backwards and forwards in front of the Tabernacle and in the presence of the people or by the waving of Aaron's hands, notes that the same word is used elsewhere of offerings of different kinds, as of gold in Exodus, and holds the symbolical meaning obvious from the concluding words of the verse.

debates: What the laying on of hands transferred: Keil argues expressly against Knobel that it was not merely a release from the nation's possession but a transfer of the obligation to serve the Lord in the persons of the first-born, Ellicott reaches nearly the same result from the sacrificial use of the phrase, Wesley speaks of the transfer of the right of ministering, and Clarke insists it meant no more than the giving up of the tribe in place of the first-born

Whether the passage bears on the people's part in appointing ministers: Clarke alone raises the question and declines to settle it, turning it instead into an argument for the maintenance of the ministry, that they who served the altar should live by the altar

How the waving was performed: Gill and Wesley say Aaron could not wave them and suppose he made the motion which they imitated, Keil takes it to have been a solemn conducting up to the altar and back, and Ellicott says the manner is simply not expressed and leaves both possibilities open

What the waving signified: Gill offers belonging to the Lord of the whole earth, readiness to serve and constant employment in service, while reporting Ainsworth's contrary supposition that it figures the troubles and afflictions of ministers; Wesley takes it of readiness to serve God wheresoever they should be

The age of the bullock: Gill reports the wise men for three years old against the inference of two from the second bullock, with others allowing four or five, while Wesley ignores the age and explains the victim by the Levites' standing in the room of the first-born
outliers: Clarke's argument for the maintenance of the ministry, that the people bound themselves to provide for men who because of their sacred service could follow no secular work
Ainsworth's supposition, reported by Gill, that the waving figures the troubles and afflictions of the ministers of God
Keil's named opponent Knobel, the only modern interlocutor in the span
Wesley's picture of the Levites waving themselves toward the several parts of the world
Ellicott's note that the same verb is used of offerings of quite different kinds, as of gold in Exodus
Gill's application that the ministers of the word should be always abounding in the work of the Lord, being always in motion

12.pericope_label: The atoning sacrifices, the separation and the exchange for the first-born

schools.summary: Gill takes the Levites' laying of hands on the heads of the bullocks, or on the head of every one of them as Aben Ezra reads the singular, as transferring their sins to the victims, since these were to make atonement for them as the latter part of the verse shows; this was a figure of the imputation of sin to Christ, taught that doctrine, and led the faith of the offerers to the sin-bearing and sin-atoning Saviour. He marks with Aben Ezra that the setting before Aaron and his sons came after atonement was made, and that they were then given to be their ministers and assistants; and he sums the separation by listing the acts that effected it, the sprinkling of the water of purification, the offering of sacrifices for them, the presenting of them before the Lord with the hands of the people upon them, the offering and waving of them before the Lord, and the setting of them before Aaron and his sons. On their going in he is careful to fix the limit: not into the sanctuary, where only the priests entered, much less into the most holy place, where only the high priest went and that but once a year, in neither of which places the Levites had anything to do, but into the court of the tabernacle. On the doubled word he offers three explanations, that given, given is repeated for confirmation, that they were twice given, first to the Lord by the children of Israel and then by the Lord to Aaron and his sons as Chaskuni has it, or, with Jarchi, that the repetition marks the different parts of their service, given for bearing and carrying the vessels of the sanctuary and given for the song, to be singers in the temple. Calvin handles the exchange as a question of equity. Lest the other tribes should complain that the number of the people was diminished, God declares that the Levites were alienated from the race of Abraham, since he had acquired them to himself when he smote all the first-born of Egypt and miraculously rescued Israel's first-born, both of men and of animals, from the common destruction, thus binding them to himself by the blessing of their redemption. But this reason would seem no longer to hold good once God, in demanding the price of redemption, set the first-born free, else he would require the same thing twice over, which would be unjust. The solution is easy: when the first-born of the twelve tribes were counted they exceeded the Levites in number, so an exchange was made, all twenty-two thousand of the first-born going free of the tribute and God taking the Levites in their place as his ministers, only two hundred and seventy-three being redeemed because that was the excess of their number above the Levites; God was thus content with just and equal terms, so as not to oppress the people by a heavy burden. Since the compensation was made only on that one particular day, it did not prevent the Israelites from owing to God their children not then born, and the law was passed that they should redeem their first-born for the future; nor was there any unfairness in the consecration of children born to the Levites, since of whatever tribe they might be descended they were already his property together with all their offspring, so that the condition of the people was not made worse by the exchange. In saying that they were given to him, God means that they were his by compact, not by gratuitous gift, and in this sense he declares that from the day in which he smote the first-born of Egypt the first-born of Israel had become his, adding that he then took the Levites, as much as to say that he only dealt with his people with respect to the time past.

Wesley glosses the setting of the Levites before Aaron as giving them to the priests, or to their service, and marks the direction of the gift, that to the Lord they were first properly offered and by him given to the priests in order to his service. Their going in he takes of the court, where they were to wait upon the priests at the altar of burnt-offering, and, at present, of the tabernacle itself, which they were to take down and set up.

Keil says the Levites were to close this transfer of themselves to the Lord with a sin-offering and burnt-offering in which they laid their hands upon the sacrificial animals, and that by this imposition of hands they made the animals their representatives, in which they presented their own bodies to the Lord as a living sacrifice well-pleasing to him. He then paraphrases the following verses as one instruction: according to the command already given, Moses was to place the Levites before Aaron and his sons and wave them as a wave-offering before the Lord, and so separate them from the midst of the children of Israel that they might be his, after which they should come to serve the tabernacle, so that the cleansing and the waving are the whole of what is required, the same reason being assigned again in the verses that follow. Ellicott keeps to the language, noting that offer them for an offering is literally wave them as a wave-offering, as in the earlier verse and again below, and explaining that the Levites were to go into the court of the Tabernacle to keep watch there, to assist the priests at the altar of burnt-offering, and to take down and set up the Tabernacle as occasion might require. On the description of them as taken instead of such as open every womb, even instead of the first-born of all the children of Israel, he says it is difficult to determine whether the second clause is an exact equivalent of the first or a limitation of it, since if it is an exact equivalent a different meaning must be assigned to the first-born from that which it commonly bears in the Pentateuch, where it appears to be restricted to the first-born son on the father's side.

debates: What the Levites' laying of hands on the bullocks effected: Gill calls it a transfer of their sins and a figure of the imputation of sin to Christ, while Keil calls it the making of the animals their representatives, in which they presented their own bodies as a living sacrifice

How far the Levites might go in: Gill draws the line hard at the court and denies them the sanctuary and the most holy place altogether, while Ellicott and Wesley add that they were to take down and set up the Tabernacle itself

Whether the redemption of the first-born charged Israel twice: Calvin raises the objection himself and answers it by the count, twenty-two thousand first-born set free against the Levites taken in their place and only the two hundred and seventy-three excess redeemed

Whether the first-born of verse 16 is an exact equivalent of such as open every womb or a limitation of it: Ellicott leaves the question open and notes that the first reading would force an unusual sense on first-born for the Pentateuch
Why the word given is doubled: Gill reports confirmation, Chaskuni's twofold giving first to the Lord and then to Aaron, and Jarchi's division between the bearing of the vessels and the song
outliers: Gill's report of Jarchi that the two givings answer to the carrying of the vessels and to the temple song
Calvin's insistence that given means belonging by compact and not by gratuitous gift
Calvin's answer to the objection that the Levites' own children were unfairly consecrated, since they were God's already whatever tribe they sprang from
Keil's compression of six verses into a single instruction, cleansing and waving being the whole of what is required
Gill's list of the six acts by which the separation was effected
Wesley's note that the Levites were offered to the Lord first and given by him to the priests, not given to the priests directly

17.pericope_label: The gift of the Levites, the averting of the plague and the atonement made for them

schools.summary: Gill reads the gift as a second giving, the Lord giving to Aaron and his sons the Levites that had first been given to him, as they were when brought before him and the children of Israel laid hands on them and they were offered before the Lord; on the earlier verses he notes that God gave up his right in the first-born and instead of them took the Levites for his use and service, and on the last that the Levites were purified from sin by the sprinkling of the sin water, or water of purification, upon them. Calvin denies that gift bears its obvious sense: it is not to be understood as such an act as that whereby a person resigns and cedes his own right to another, but when God devotes them to the ministry of the sanctuary he desires that they should have a leader and master, that they may be directed by Aaron and obey his commands. The end of the verse, he says, teaches that this is done for the advantage and profit of the whole people, whence there was no room for ill-will towards them unless the people should perhaps be annoyed that God had taken measures for their welfare; and the advantage is twofold, since they were to be the intercessors or ministers of reconciliation, either sense being appropriate, and since as guardians of the sanctuary they would prevent the Israelites from bringing destruction upon themselves by their rash approach to it. On the inauguration he observes that the Levites are set in their proper order because their condition was inferior, and that the sons of Moses and their descendants were placed in this lower rank and excluded from all expectation of the priesthood, so that the ingratitude of the whole people and especially of the tribe of Levi was all the more base when they presumptuously sought the honour from which Moses had shut out his own children for ever; it was no ordinary act of obedience in him to execute what God had appointed, Aaron is mentioned because he consecrated the Levites in right of his priesthood, and the people's consent is merely commended, a virtue which only increased their ignominy afterwards when they sought to overthrow the divine decree of which they had approved. On the purifying he says that since washing was required of all private individuals much less would it be allowable for the Levites to handle the sacred things unless first purified, and that their presentation by the hands of Aaron was a shadowing forth by symbol of the truth which at length shone out at the coming of Christ, for it had been of old predicted by the prophets that in the renovation of the Church those who had hitherto been but of the multitude should become Levites; by this figure God would declare that none even of his elect servants would be approved of and accepted by him unless sanctified by the one Priest, and thence an atonement is joined with their offering, in order that the Levites might be pure.

Clarke adds only a cross-reference on the redemption of the first-born, but on the atonement he presses the point hard: though the Levites had been most solemnly consecrated to the Lord's service, and though all legal washings and purifications were duly performed on the occasion, yet they could not approach God till an atonement had been made for them; and how strange is it, after all these significations of the will and purpose of God relative to man, that any priest or any people will attempt to draw nigh to God without an atonement, since as sure as God hath spoken it there is no entrance into the holiest but through the blood of Jesus. Wesley explains the service of Israel as serving God in their stead, doing what otherwise the people had been obliged to do in their own persons, and is careful about the atonement they are said to make: not by offering sacrifices, which the priests alone might do, but by assisting the priests in that expiatory work and by a diligent performance of all the parts of their office, whereby God was pleased both with them and with the people. The clause about the plague he takes as the reason why God appointed them to serve in the tabernacle, that they might guard it and not suffer any of the people to come near it or meddle with holy things, which if they did would certainly bring a plague upon them.

Ellicott renders as a gift by the Hebrew given, as in the earlier verse, and explains the clause about the plague as a matter of competence: the appointment of the Levites in the place of the first-born was calculated to insure the reverent and orderly discharge of the duties of the Sanctuary, and to operate as a safeguard against those sins of omission and commission into which the first-born would have been more likely to be betrayed, and which would have provoked the divine wrath against the Israelites generally. Keil fixes the Levitical period of service at twenty-five years of age and upwards to the fiftieth year, so that from twenty-five the Levite should come to do service at the work of the tabernacle, and at fifty should return from the service of the work and not work any further but only serve his brethren at the tabernacle in keeping charge, that is, help them to look after its furniture; charge, as distinguished from work, signifies the oversight of all the furniture of the tabernacle, while work applies to laborious service.

debates: What the word gift means: Gill takes it of a second giving, the Levites given to the Lord and by him to Aaron, while Calvin denies that it is any resignation or cession of right and makes it the appointment of a leader and master over them

Why the appointment averted a plague: Ellicott makes it a matter of the orderly and competent discharge of sanctuary duties, Wesley makes it guard duty keeping the people from the holy things, and Calvin makes it twofold, intercession and guardianship together

In what sense the Levites made atonement: Wesley denies that they offered sacrifices, which the priests alone might do, and confines it to assisting the priests and diligence in office, while Calvin allows either intercessors or ministers of reconciliation

Whether the exclusion of Moses' sons aggravates the later revolt: Calvin alone raises it, arguing that the tribe of Levi sought presumptuously the very honour from which Moses had shut out his own children for ever

What the ceremonies could and could not do: Clarke insists that consecration and all the legal washings still left the Levites unable to approach God without atonement, while Calvin reads the presentation by Aaron's hands as a figure of sanctification by the one Priest
outliers: Clarke's application that there is no entrance into the holiest but through the blood of Jesus
Calvin's use of the prophetic promise that in the renovation of the Church those who had been but of the multitude should become Levites
Calvin's note that the people's consent is merely commended, and that this virtue increased their ignominy when they later sought to overthrow the decree they had approved
Keil's distinction between charge, the oversight of the furniture, and work, the laborious service, which fixes what the Levite over fifty still did
Wesley's definition of the service of Israel as doing what the people would otherwise have been obliged to do in their own persons
Calvin's remark that there was no room for ill-will towards the Levites unless the people were annoyed that God had taken measures for their welfare

22.pericope_label: The entrance on service, the ages of twenty-five and fifty, and the keeping of the charge

schools.summary: Gill says the Levites went into the court of the tabernacle, having been at the door of it while the rites and ceremonies of their consecration were performed, and that the Lord fixed the time of their entrance on their service and of their leaving it at the same time as he gave the instructions about their consecration. On the ministry of the older Levites he says they gave advice, instructed younger Levites and did lighter service, reporting Jarchi that they returned to shutting of doors, singing and loading wagons, though the last especially seems to him too burdensome; the keeping of the charge he explains of the tabernacle, to watch and observe that no stranger or unclean person enter into it, which they were capable of at fifty and upwards, and the doing of no service he explains of what was heavy and laborious, the whole respecting ancient men as Aben Ezra notes, though it may include both their entrance on their work and their cessation from it. Calvin takes the summary verse as the seal of the whole: in the type nothing was omitted relative to the ancient priesthood which pertains to the legitimate service of God, the main point in which is obedience, and thence the purity which flows from it; the Levites are said to have done their service before Aaron because they humbly submitted themselves to the yoke and allowed themselves to be controlled by the will of the priest, since God had so enjoined. But the progress of the history, he adds, will presently shew how prone man's nature is to rebellion, whence it arises that the end does not always correspond with the beginning, but that sad and unhappy conclusions sometimes follow successful commencements. On the ages he finds very good reason for both provisions. If they had been admitted in early youth their levity might have greatly detracted from the reverence due to sacred things, not only because those whose manhood is not yet mature are generally given to pleasure and intemperance, but because by negligence, or levity, or want of thought, or ignorance and error they might have made many grievous mistakes in the service of God; and as they were by no means fitted to exercise their charge until they should have attained prudence and gravity, so also, lest they should fail from old age, it was right that they should be seasonably dismissed, their duties being laborious and such as demanded bodily strength. Applying this to the pastoral office he holds that none should be chosen to it except such as have already given proofs of their moderation, and that those who diligently devote themselves to it should not be unreasonably pressed upon, nor should more be required of them than their ability can bear, for some foolishly count their years, as if it were a sin to choose a pastor before his twenty-fourth year, although he might be otherwise fully provided with the necessary qualifications.

Clarke settles the discrepancy of ages by referring to his earlier note, where the two terms of twenty-five and thirty years are reconciled. On the older Levites he says they were no longer obliged to perform any laborious service but acted as general directors and counsellors, and were therefore to be near the camp, to sing praises to God, and to see that no stranger or unclean person was permitted to enter, as the Jews and many other persons have understood the place. He then draws two applications. If it required so much legal purity to fit the Levites for their work in the tabernacle, it cannot require less spiritual purity to fit ministers of the Gospel to proclaim the righteousness of the Most High and administer the sacred ordinances to the flock of Christ; and if these Levites, who were only typical men, must be without spot as the priests were without blemish, a Christian minister requires no ordinary measure of holiness for an acceptable and profitable discharge of his office. And if the Christian ministry is established to prepare men for the kingdom of God, of the holiness of which the purity of the camp was but a faint emblem, no man can expect to enter that place of blessedness who has not his heart sprinkled from an evil conscience and his body washed with pure water, and his life agreeable to the sacred precepts of the Gospel; if the law of Moses were more read in reference to the Gospel, the Gospel itself and its requisitions would be much better understood, for Antinomianism is more general among religious people than is usually imagined, and multitudes of all denominations expect to enter the kingdom of God without any proper preparation for the place, though without holiness none shall see the Lord. Wesley says only that the older Levites ministered in the tabernacle by way of advice, and assistance in lesser and easier works.

Keil argues that both the heading and the final clause by which this law relating to the Levites' period of service is bounded, and its position immediately after their induction into office, show unmistakeably that the law was binding for all time and was intended to apply to the standing service of the Levites at the sanctuary, and consequently that it is not at variance with the instructions of the earlier chapter to muster the Levites between thirty and fifty years of age and organise them for the transport of the Tabernacle; he glosses the term rendered charge as attendance upon an official post. Ellicott sets out three ways of taking the regulation. It may refer to the age at which the Levites were to enter upon their duties after the people had taken possession of the land of Canaan, and appears to have remained in force until the time of David, who substituted the age of twenty for that of twenty-five, because the necessity of carrying the Tabernacle and its furniture from place to place, which arose but seldom after the entrance into Canaan, finally ceased after the removal of the ark to Mount Zion, the time of service during the wanderings having been from thirty to fifty, when the constant removal of the Tabernacle required men in the full vigour of life. Or, since the chronological order of events is not always observed in this book, the directions may have been given at a later period and inserted here in connection with the account of the appointment of the Levites. Or it is quite possible that from the first the Levites entered upon the lighter parts of their office at twenty-five but were not employed before thirty in the more onerous duties of removing the Tabernacle or bearing the sacred vessels on their shoulders, as in the case of the Kohathites. He renders to wait upon the service literally as to war the warfare, or to serve the military service, and similarly in the following verse he shall return from the warfare of the service; and on the last verse he marks a clear distinction between the service which involved heavy manual labour in carrying the furniture of the Tabernacle and in slaughtering the victims, and the charge or oversight of the furniture and the vessels of the Sanctuary.

debates: How the age of twenty-five is to be squared with the muster from thirty in the earlier chapter: Clarke refers to his own earlier reconciliation, Keil argues from the heading and closing formula that this law governs the standing service and so does not conflict with a rule made for the transport, and Ellicott offers three possibilities and settles on none

Whether the regulation was for the wilderness or for Canaan: Ellicott takes it as most likely a rule for the settled land, in force until David lowered the age to twenty, while Keil takes it as binding for all time from the moment of the Levites' induction

What the Levite over fifty still did: Gill and Clarke agree on advice, oversight and the exclusion of strangers, but Gill objects to Jarchi's inclusion of loading wagons as too burdensome, and Wesley reduces it to advice and assistance in easier works

Why the two limits were set: Calvin argues both from prudence rather than from the text, the young being given to levity and error and the old failing in bodily strength, and turns the argument on those who foolishly count a pastor's years
What distinction the word charge carries: Ellicott makes it a distinction of kind from the heavy manual labour of carrying and slaughtering, while Keil glosses it as attendance upon an official post
outliers: Calvin's warning that the progress of the history will shew how prone man's nature is to rebellion, so that sad conclusions sometimes follow successful commencements
Calvin's complaint that some foolishly count years, as if it were a sin to choose a pastor before his twenty-fourth year
Clarke's charge that Antinomianism is more general among religious people than is usually imagined
Clarke's rule that if the law of Moses were more read in reference to the Gospel, the Gospel itself would be much better understood
Ellicott's literal rendering of the service as warring the warfare, and of the dismissal as returning from the warfare of the service
Gill's report of Jarchi that the older Levites returned to shutting the doors, singing and loading wagons, with his own objection to the last
Ellicott's note that David substituted twenty for twenty-five once the ark had been removed to Mount Zion
